figures.caption: Figure 2 DANCE yields a threefold improvement in event-based F1 over all baselines. A. Performance averaged across subjects and datasets (Mean ± SEM) comparing baselines and ablations against the proposed DANCE model. Statistical significance via Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMM; Section B.4.2) is indicated as follows: ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, and ∗∗∗p < 0.001. B. Normalized radar profiles showing relative averaged performance per subject across individual datasets. Axes are normalized to the best-performing method for each dataset. Numeric annotations indicate the absolute score of DANCE at each vertex, and the outer ring groups datasets by task category.

Figure A.1 A. F1event of DANCE as a function of the IoU acceptance threshold τ , one curve per dataset (coloured by task domain). B. Detection quality (F1det, class-agnostic, ↑ better) versus temporal precision (∆ctr, center-point error in seconds, log scale, ← better) for DANCE (coloured) against the best non-ablation rival (grey). If the arrow points to the upper left, it means DANCE dominates on both axes. The arrow runs from the best baseline to the DANCE model.
Table B.1 Additional information on the experimental datasets.

Figure 3 DANCE yields qualitatively superior event predictions than baseline architectures. Visualization of selected session segments comparing three architectures: U-Net, CBraMod, and our proposed model. Ground truth (GT) events are depicted alongside predictions from the respective models. Solid outlines indicate true positives, while dashed outlines denote false positives with respect to F1event. Colors represent distinct classes. F1event (F1e) and F1sample (F1s) are shown on the right for each portion.

Figure A.4 Qualitative timelines onmotor-imagery datasets. One row per method (top: ground truth; below: DANCE, CBraMod, U-Net). Coloured rectangles encode the predicted event class; solid borders mark predictions matching a ground-truth event (class and IoU ≥ 0.5), dashed borders mark mismatches. Left: BNCI2014 (4 classes), 83–153 s of one subject. Right: BNCI2015 (2 classes), 200–500 s of one subject. Per-row F1event (F1e) and F1sample (F1s) on this window are reported on the right.

Figure 4 DANCE establishes a new state-of-the-art for clinical seizure monitoring on the TUSZ dataset andmatches onsetinformed approaches on BNCI2014. A. Benchmarking of DANCE against existing literature and ablation baselines using the F1seizure metric. Scores are reported from Wu et al. (2025). DANCE is evaluated across 3 model seeds. TUSZ has a fixed test split. B. Intra-session performance on the BNCI2014 dataset for DANCE and the MOABB (Chevallier et al., 2024) benchmark. Standard deviation is reported.

Figure B.1 Temporal smoothing fails to improve event-based performance for baseline architectures. The impact of the gap-filling parameter τ on the F1event score for baseline methods (ATCNet, U-Net, CBraMod). For each τ ∈ [0, 0.125] s (x-axis), disjoint predictions of the same class are merged into a single continuous event if separated by a gap of ≤ τ . Results are shown for the Pinet (left) and Broderick (right) datasets.

Figure A.2 DANCE is robust to the DETR lossweights. Mean F1sample (blue) and F1event (green) over BI2014b, BNCI2014 and Broderick (5-fold CV per dataset) for four configurations of the DETR localization and classification loss weights (λIoU, λclass). Error bars are the SEM across datasets. The default configuration (5, 1) used in every other experiment is highlighted with a thick border. Performance varies by less than 0.05 F1 across the swept range.

Figure 5 DANCE queries dynamically specialize in specific temporal regions and event classes. Visualization of the temporal distribution of predictions across selected queries. For each query row, the outer envelope corresponds to when the query activates. This is the total density of predictions. The colored bands indicate what it predicts. The stacked inner colored bands decompose this density by predicted class (most frequent at the base). A sharp, narrow envelope indicates temporal specialization, while a dominant color indicates class specialization.
Table 1 Summary of experimental datasets. Mean values are displayed.

Figure A.3 validates this design on the phoneme case, the dataset closest to the resolution bound: at W = 8 s (3.4 tokens/event) DANCE is at its optimum, while doubling W pushes n̄ past the three-token cutoff and F1event collapses regardless of how queries are allocated. The fixed-NQevent baseline falls to 18%, and scaling NQevent in proportion to W drops further to ∼ 1%.

Table A.1 Decoupled detection and localization metrics. F1detect measures class-agnostic detection (IoU≥0.5). F1event adds class awareness. ∆center is the mean temporal error of true positives in seconds. Best rival is the highest-scoring non-ablation baseline per dataset.
